results.note: p. 295, right column, 5th paragraph of the opening section: association 'perfectly clear-cut and beyond what we would care to attribute to the play of chance'; Hill asks what to consider before deciding causation is the most likely interpretation.

results.corrected_extracted: The coronary thrombosis death rate in smokers was no more than twice that of non-smokers, possibly less; though there is good evidence to support causation, Hill finds it much easier in this case to think of features of life going hand in hand with smoking, such as lack of exercise or diet, that might conceivably be the real underlying cause or at least an important contributor; the lung cancer death rate, nine to ten times that of non-smokers (p. 295), would need a feature so closely tied to smoking and to the amount smoked that it should be easy to detect.
results.note: Place right. The anchor dropped Hill's qualifier 'Though there is good evidence to support causation' (for coronary thrombosis too) and the hedge 'conceivably ... at the least'; restored.

p. 1180, right column, 5th paragraph of the section. Berkson's own example is diabetes with cholecystitis; the authors' 'similarly' example (depression with alcohol abuse) is hedged 'may be more likely'; the anchor does not overstate it.

p. 299, left column, paragraph after (9) Analogy: 'None of my nine viewpoints can bring indisputable evidence' and none 'can be required as a sine qua non'; no hard-and-fast rules; the 'equally, or more, likely' question is printed.

pp. 298-299, (8) Experiment: dust reduced, oils changed, persons stop smoking; 'the strongest support for the causation hypothesis may be revealed'. Hill opens with 'Occasionally it is possible'; the 'may' is kept.

results.corrected_extracted: In occupational medicine, Hill says, more often than not general medical knowledge gives no guidance, and we depend on observing and counting defined events and then looking for what went before them, that is, on associations. In this passage he says nothing about drugs, and gives no share.
results.note: Place right (p. 295, 3rd paragraph). Hill says 'we are dependent upon' observation, not that knowledge 'starts from' it; and the paper does mention drugs elsewhere (thalidomide, p. 299; a drug for morning sickness, p. 300), so 'in this passage'.

results.corrected_extracted: For several diseases, including alcoholism and opiate addiction (the paper's terms), clinicians sample the people ill at a given moment (a prevalence or census sample), which is biased toward long-lasting cases because each case's chance of being in it is proportional to how long it lasts, whereas research samples tend to come closer to everyone who ever develops the condition; the authors call this bias the clinician's illusion, and say part of the disagreement about long-term prognosis may be attributable to this difference in the populations sampled.
results.note: Abstract, p. 1178. The abstract says 'research samples tend to more nearly represent', not 'follow-up research comes closer'; restored 'tend to' and the hedge 'Part of this disagreement may be attributable'.

p. 1180, section's 1st-3rd paragraphs (left column into right): 'likely not to be representative'; recovery without treatment using personal and social resources, 'likely to have a better prognosis'; entrants 'likely to have been ill longer'.

p. 1181: 1st paragraph (useful when conclusions are limited to patients seen in services like the source) and 11th paragraph (without careful specification of treatment history and selection, the population is unknown).

p. 1179, 7th body paragraph ('not our intent to come to any substantive conclusions'); p. 1180, section paragraph 4 ('not trying to present or evaluate empirical evidence'); Fig 1 is a 'hypothetical disease' with a 'posited' distribution.

p. 296, right column, (2) Consistency, 4th paragraph (Heady 1958). Hill's wording is 'perforated ulcer' and 'that fallacy'; 'Bears on who ends up in a hospital sample' is the writer's own gloss, a fair one.

results.corrected_extracted: Hill's temporality viewpoint: which came first. His examples: a diet may lead to a disease, or the early stages of the disease may lead to the diet; a job may promote tuberculosis, or the people who choose that work may be more liable to it or already infected. He calls the question particularly relevant to diseases of slow development, and says this temporal problem may not arise often but certainly needs to be remembered, particularly with selective factors at work in industry.
results.note: Place right (pp. 297-298). Restored Hill's hedge that the temporal problem 'may not arise often' and his scope (diseases of slow development; selective factors in industry).

results.corrected_extracted: The coronary thrombosis death rate in smokers was no more than twice that of non-smokers, possibly less; though there is good evidence to support causation, Hill finds it much easier in this case to think of features of life going hand in hand with smoking, such as lack of exercise or diet, that might conceivably be the real underlying cause or at least an important contributor; the lung cancer death rate, nine to ten times that of non-smokers (p. 295), would need a feature so closely tied to smoking and to the amount smoked that it should be easy to detect.
results.note: Same anchor as n 2: restored 'Though there is good evidence to support causation' and the hedge 'conceivably ... at the least'.

results.corrected_extracted: In a sample of people currently ill (a prevalence sample, which overrepresents the long-term ill) compared with controls, there is likely to be no way to separate characteristics that affect how long an illness lasts from those causally connected to it; the authors keep this distinct from the more familiar difficulty, in such samples, of distinguishing causes of a disease from its consequences.
results.note: Place right (p. 1181, 5th-6th paragraphs). The source speaks of 'the difficulty ... in distinguishing causes ... from consequences', not that samples 'cannot tell'; and says the problem 'needs to be kept distinct from' it.

p. 298, left column, (5) Biological gradient, 1st-2nd paragraphs: rises linearly with cigarettes smoked daily, 'adds a very great deal'; measure of the environment often difficult, 'we should invariably seek it'. Last sentence is the writer's fair gloss.
p. 296, right column, (2) Consistency, 2nd paragraph, as stated; 'may sometimes be answered only by a repetition' kept as hedged.

p. 299: Tests of Significance 1st paragraph (left) and 5th paragraph (right, 'innumerable situations in which they are totally unnecessary'). 'Often' is a fair rendering; 'proof' is in quotation marks in Hill.
p. 300, left column, top: 'far too often we deduce "no difference" from "no significant difference"' (paragraph begins p. 299 'Of course I exaggerate').
p. 296, left column, (1) Strength, 3rd-4th paragraphs. Ratios 8, 20, 32 to 1 recomputed from 0.57, 1.39, 2.27 over 0.07 per 1,000 (8.1, 19.9, 32.4); Snow 71 vs 5 per 10,000 houses = 14.2.

p. 296, right column, (2) Consistency, 1st-3rd paragraphs: 29 retrospective and 7 prospective inquiries (found by the Surgeon-General's Advisory Committee); 'not due to some constant error or fallacy that permeates every inquiry'.

results.corrected_extracted: Repetition has limits: a bias built into a design is not removed, and not necessarily revealed, by any number of exact repetitions (Heady's hospital example); the same results from precisely the same form of inquiry will not invariably greatly strengthen the original evidence, while Hill puts a good deal of weight on similar results reached in quite different ways; and where repetition is absent or impossible a unique observation can still convince (South Wales nickel refiners, 1929-1938: 16 lung cancer deaths against about one expected, 11 nasal cancer deaths against a fraction of one).
results.note: Place right (pp. 296-297). Hill: repetitions 'would remove or necessarily reveal' nothing, i.e. not necessarily revealed (the anchor said never revealed); 'add less' replaced by his hedge 'will not invariably greatly strengthen'. Numbers confirmed.
